claims.statement: Xianrendong pottery-bearing contexts were dated to approximately 20,000–19,000 calibrated years BP, long before farming; this dates surviving use, not the invention of pottery.

sources.supports: Associated bone/charcoal dates and micromorphological checks of the deposits.

claims.counterevidence: The dated materials are associated deposits; some strata were affected by small-scale bioturbation.
claims.inference_limits: No first inventor, unique origin, or regional prevalence follows from this site.

test.reason: Reports contextual dating, not a causal explanation of adoption.

claims.statement: Meroe replica smelts improved after changes in ore, air delivery and operation, demonstrating coupled operating constraints rather than the sufficiency of a copied furnace shape.

sources.supports: Failed/low-yield trials, changes to ores and bellows, viable later operation and explicit experimental limitations.

claims.counterevidence: Parameters changed together; some later successes lacked detailed records.
claims.inference_limits: Modern reconstructed feasibility does not identify the unique ancient process or provide an ancient output series.

test.mechanism_chain: Suitable ore plus adjusted blast/charging and operator coordination -> better reduction/slag behaviour -> more workable products in replica trials.
test.strongest_rival: Different modern operating choices could also succeed; apparent improvement could result from one unisolated variable rather than the whole historical reconstruction.
test.discriminating_observation: Controlled replication changing one parameter at a time, matching archaeological residues and retaining detailed mass balances.
test.evidence_sought_found: MAT-S06 Tables 2–4 and Lessons Learned record failed/low-yield runs and improved combinations; authors flag anecdotal later data.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Joint changes prevent attribution to each input; viability is demonstrated only for tested modern configurations, not a unique ancient procedure.

claims.statement: Hosler proposed South/Central American transmission into West Mexico combined with local technical transformation; this is a claim about selective recombination, not passive copying.

sources.supports: Two proposed phases of technical links and explicit local reinterpretation.

claims.counterevidence: Only abstract read; dates differ between the 1988 and 1995 formulations. Similarity alone cannot exclude convergence.
claims.inference_limits: Transfer route and carriers remain unverified here; neither isolation nor a complete imported package is assumed.

test.mechanism_chain: Interregional contact -> movement of know-how/components -> local recombination -> distinctive West Mexican production.
test.strongest_rival: Convergence from similar resources/tasks can create similarities without the proposed transfer; object movement alone may not transmit skills.
test.discriminating_observation: Diagnostic production sequences, intermediate chronology, source/provenance and contact evidence evaluated together.
test.evidence_sought_found: MAT-S11 abstract proposes two transmission phases and transformations; detailed supporting catalogue unavailable.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Neither routes, carriers nor first dates independently verified; similarity alone fits several accounts.

claims.statement: Incompletely reacted glass batch on Ile-Ife crucibles directly strengthens the case for local primary glassmaking, while recipe uniqueness alone cannot establish an origin independent of all external ideas.

sources.locator: accepted manuscript pp. 2–4, Laboratory analysis and Implications
sources.supports: Residual quartz/feldspar, new reaction phases and heterogeneous glass distinguish raw-batch melting from only remelting finished imports.
Locally compatible recipe and participation in exchange.

claims.counterevidence: Museum-store fragments lack newly excavated sealed contexts; authors advance a stronger autonomous-origin interpretation.
claims.inference_limits: Local primary production is better established than the exact invention date, transmission history or subsequent disappearance.

test.reason: Identifies material evidence of a production operation; does not claim an adoption cause or independent-invention mechanism.

sources.title: Early Pottery at 20,000 Years Ago in Xianrendong Cave, China
sources.locator: Science 336:1696–1700; inspected pottery description, dating/context argument, Tables 1–2 and discussion through author-uploaded full-text extraction. DOI 10.1126/science.1218643.
sources.scope_limit: Dates associated deposits, not an invention event; supplementary micromorphology and dating files not independently acquired. No regional diffusion denominator.
sources.evidence_lineage: Original Xianrendong dating/context study combines 1993–2000 excavations and earlier dates with 2009 resampling; 45 dated samples discussed, including 13 from the reopened profiles. This is one site archive, not independent replications.

sources.title: Iron Smelting in Sudan: Experimental Archaeology at The Royal City of Meroe
sources.locator: Journal of Field Archaeology 43(5):399–416; introduction, experimental campaigns, Tables 2–4, Lessons Learned and Conclusion, pp. 412–415. PDF acquired locally and text inspected.
sources.scope_limit: Replica reflects later/post-Meroitic workshops; multiple parameters changed together. Later results described as anecdotal without detailed quantification. Demonstrates a viable reconstruction, not unique ancient operation.
sources.evidence_lineage: Original modern Meroe smelting experiments informed by archaeological workshops and local materials. Shares project context and inherited chronology with MAT-S07, but the experimental dataset differs from its charcoal analysis.

sources.title: Ancient West Mexican Metallurgy: South and Central American Origins and West Mexican Transformations
sources.locator: American Anthropologist 90(4):832–855; publisher abstract and bibliographic information inspected.
sources.scope_limit: Diffusion argument not independently audited beyond abstract. Its circa AD 800 starting date differs from the circa AD 600 framework in the later paper; neither is used as a securely identified first invention.
sources.evidence_lineage: Abstract from Hosler’s West Mexican research programme proposing external technical roots and local changes. The analytical corpus and transfer argument were not fully inspected; this is not independent corroboration of MAT-S10.

sources.title: Chemical analysis of glass beads from Igbo Olokun, Ile-Ife (SW Nigeria): New light on raw materials, production, and interregional interactions
sources.locator: Journal of Archaeological Science 90:92–105; sections 2, 3.4, 4.1–4.3 and 5; Table 3 and discussion of sampling and disturbed deposits. DOI 10.1016/j.jas.2017.12.005.
sources.scope_limit: 52 beads selected to cover visible diversity, about 0.5% of excavated assemblage; no statistical population sample. Disturbed deposits and no intact furnace in these units limit chronology and organisation.
sources.evidence_lineage: Original chemical analysis of 52 selected beads from 2011–2012 Igbo Olokun excavations, alongside comparisons with older collections. Shares excavation and researchers with MAT-S12. Earlier comparative glass databases are inherited, not all independently audited.

sources.title: Semi-finished glass from Ile-Ife, Nigeria: implications for the archaeology of glass in sub-Saharan Africa
sources.locator: Accepted manuscript pp. 1–4; sections 2016 and 2017 investigations, Semi-finished glass, Laboratory analysis, Implications and concluding remarks.
sources.scope_limit: Three museum-store fragments recorded from Igbo Olokun, not newly excavated in sealed contexts. Strong primary-production evidence; unique recipe does not by itself exclude transferred ideas or workers.
sources.evidence_lineage: Original examination of three museum-store crucible fragments recorded from Igbo Olokun. Distinct specimens strengthen the same local-production argument as MAT-S12–S13; common site attribution, investigators and interpretive framework limit independence.

cases.title: Forager pottery: early occurrence and later use in China and Japan
cases.period: Approximately 20,000–19,000 cal BP at Xianrendong; Japanese comparison approximately 14,460–8,000 cal BP
cases.summary: Early vessels and later Japanese residue evidence separate technical occurrence from the conditions and purposes of wider use.

stages.invention: No inventor or single origin identified; Xianrendong provides an early surviving occurrence.
stages.feasibility: Formed and fired vessels plus use traces demonstrate workable ceramic containers; production frequency remains unknown.
stages.deployment: Forager contexts at Xianrendong and sampled Jōmon vessels document actual use.
stages.diffusion: Japanese sites provide regional functional comparison, not proof that the technique diffused from Xianrendong.
stages.scaling: Early Holocene expansion is reported qualitatively; sample size is not a production denominator.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Late Pleistocene use could remain limited; no evidence here that all forager households adopted pots.
stages.displacement/reversal: No complete replacement of other cooking/storage methods is demonstrated.

mechanisms: mobility and transport costs as untested hypotheses
cases.counterevidence: Residue preservation, site selection and associated dating constrain interpretation.

episode.technology_configuration: Fired vessel pottery at Xianrendong; separately, residue-bearing Incipient/Initial Jōmon ceramics
episode.task: Containment and probable cooking at Xianrendong; aquatic-resource processing in sampled Japanese vessels
episode.population: Occupants whose debris survived at Xianrendong and users of sampled vessels at 46 Japanese sites; household populations unknown
episode.interval: Approximately 20,000–19,000 cal BP at Xianrendong; Japanese comparison approximately 14,460–8,000 cal BP
contemporary_alternatives: Non-ceramic containers and direct cooking are candidate alternatives; availability and task-by-task use not documented in the inspected papers
Existing local stone, bone and shell tools coexist; they are not equivalent container substitutes
episode.adoption_measure: Dated occurrence at one Chinese site; Japanese chemical assignments among 801 selected samples, including 722 yielding interpreted lipids. No denominator of households, all pots or meals.
episode.observation_limits: Two separated regional subepisodes, not a demonstrated transmission chain. Associated dates, deposition, preservation and selection limit prevalence and functional inference.

actors.chooser: Unknown: prehistoric vessel makers/users are inferred from remains, with no records of household decisions.
actors.payer: Unknown: clay, fuel and labour inputs existed, but household/gender ownership or resource obligations are not identified.
actors.operator_maintainer: Vessel-forming, firing and cooking practitioners; identities, maintenance roles and unpaid-work allocation unknown.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Other household members and fuel/clay collectors are possible affected parties, not identified groups in these data.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Unknown; archaeological occurrence cannot distinguish voluntary household choice, dependence or imposed work.

labour.tasks: Forming, tempering, firing and cooking tasks; no evidence of paid employment or a distinct potter occupation.
labour.entry_barriers: Practical ceramic skill and access to clay/fuel; apprenticeship and social exclusion unknown.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Unknown: no direct evidence of ownership, bargaining or gains.
labour.transition: Long temporal gaps between occurrences; no individual/cohort transition evidence.
labour.distribution: No measured livelihood gains or losses by gender, class or household.
labour.evidence_limit: Residues and sherds cannot determine labour hours, wages, gender division or welfare.

cases.title: Meroe and Hamadab: workable ironmaking and long-lived fuel selection
cases.period: Iron production attested from at least seventh–sixth centuries BCE into the first millennium CE; experiments model later/post-Meroitic workshops
cases.summary: Replica smelts reveal operating constraints, while charcoal identifies persistent fuel selection without resolving landscape sustainability.

stages.invention: No claim about first African ironmaking or external versus independent origins.
stages.feasibility: Archaeological waste proves ancient production; modern experiments identify one viable reconstructed operating range.
stages.deployment: Workshops and slag accumulations demonstrate sustained local operation.
stages.diffusion: Destination and social distribution of much output remain unresolved.
stages.scaling: Large and variable accumulations imply substantial production but do not yield a verified annual series.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Unsuitable experimental ores and operating combinations fail; ancient non-user groups are not measured.
stages.displacement/reversal: Production extends beyond Kushite political transformations; final cessation and its causes are not established here.

cases.counterevidence: Experimental changes are not cleanly isolated; charcoal survival cannot rule out damage elsewhere in a supply catchment.

episode.technology_configuration: Ancient Meroe/Hamadab ironmaking and selected fuels; separately modern replicas of later/post-Meroitic workshops
episode.task: Producing iron/steel stock; ultimate ancient product destinations not established
episode.population: Ancient producers represented by workshop/debris and charcoal samples; modern experimental teams provide operating evidence, not ancient actor testimony
episode.interval: Iron production attested from at least seventh–sixth centuries BCE into the first millennium CE; experiments model later/post-Meroitic workshops
contemporary_alternatives: Different local ores and charging/blast configurations tested experimentally
Alternative charcoal taxa occur in non-metallurgical contexts; ancient metallurgical substitution is not demonstrated
Imported iron or semi-products are potential consumer alternatives but unmeasured
episode.adoption_measure: Workshop/debris presence and charcoal composition; experimental success/failure and yields under stated modern conditions. No ancient annual output or adoption-population denominator.
episode.observation_limits: Long-lived deposits are time aggregates; modern experiments cannot substitute for ancient labour/demand evidence; charcoal may be imported.

actors.chooser: Ancient smelters demonstrably selected fuel; who controlled production targets is unknown. Modern experimenters chose trial parameters.
actors.payer: Ancient institutional or household funding unknown; modern experiments are not evidence of ancient financing.
actors.operator_maintainer: Ore preparers, charcoal suppliers, furnace builders, smelters and bellows operators; later forging/repair labour incompletely traced.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Local or distant fuel-source communities and product users; no measured harms/benefit distribution.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Unknown for ancient workers and suppliers; royal-centre context is not proof of coercion.

labour.tasks: Coordination of ore preparation, fuel production, furnace construction, bellows and smelting; ancient paid/unpaid status unknown.
labour.entry_barriers: Tacit operating skill and suitable ore/fuel; modern expert trial difficulty demonstrates process demands, not ancient social exclusivity.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Unknown; debris does not identify owners, wage setting or bargaining.
labour.transition: Ancient multi-century continuity; modern trials are learning sequences, not ancient labour-transition evidence.
labour.distribution: No group-level wages, exposure or welfare measures.
labour.evidence_limit: Cannot turn reconstructed yields into ancient employment, working hours or coercion rates.

cases.title: West Mexican metals: sound, colour and selective technical transfer
cases.period: Approximately 600/800 CE to early sixteenth century; differing starting dates in inspected scholarship
cases.summary: Studies identify technical uses beyond hardness and propose transmission with regional reinterpretation; this case is access-limited.

stages.invention: No earliest inventor established; reported 600/800 CE dates are not merged into a single secure first.
stages.feasibility: Alloy and fabrication knowledge is described by the original researcher; underlying object catalogue not independently reanalysed.
stages.deployment: Tools, bells and sheet ornaments are attested in the studies.
stages.diffusion: Proposed links with Ecuador, Colombia, lower Central America and later Peru; abstract-level access limits evaluation.
stages.scaling: No verified production volume or consumer denominator in inspected material.
stages.non-adoption/niche: No case is made that absence of a Eurasian-style iron transition meant failure or lack of sophisticated metallurgy.
stages.displacement/reversal: Colonial-period change is outside the inspected evidence; no automatic technological replacement asserted.

cases.counterevidence: Only abstracts of Hosler 1988/1995 acquired; symbolic meanings, route and exact chronology require full-text follow-up.

episode.technology_configuration: West Mexican copper-alloy bells, ornaments and tools, with proposed South/Central American technical links
episode.task: Sound, visual appearance, status/ritual action and practical tool functions; meanings varied and require further audit
episode.population: Artefacts and social settings discussed in Hosler’s studies; detailed collections and adopter population not independently inspected
episode.interval: Approximately 600/800 CE to early sixteenth century; differing starting dates in inspected scholarship
contemporary_alternatives: Different metals/alloys and fabrication routes named in the studies
Other sounding, ornamental and tool materials are possible alternatives, but comparative access/use not established here
episode.adoption_measure: Qualitative abstract-level descriptions; no production or adoption-rate measure. Circa AD 600 and AD 800 starting frameworks remain distinguished.
episode.observation_limits: Abstract access cannot support object-frequency claims, complete carrier routes or exact ethnographic/ethnohistoric interpretation; elite symbolism may be overrepresented.

actors.chooser: Smiths, patrons and ritual users are candidate choosers; roles cannot be audited from abstracts.
actors.payer: Unknown; neither status associations nor technically elaborate objects reveal exact payer.
actors.operator_maintainer: Metalworkers and object users; mining, repair and maintenance organisation unavailable in inspected text.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Workers and non-elite households may be affected, but their experience is absent from inspected evidence.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Unknown; symbolic importance does not establish voluntary participation or coercion.

labour.tasks: Casting/working copper alloys and producing sounding/visual objects; task list inferred, no employment series.
labour.entry_barriers: Knowledge and material access; institutional barriers unknown due limited access.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Unknown; elite/ritual consumption does not itself identify artisan power or ownership.
labour.transition: No individual/cohort transition evidence; even initial chronology differs between abstracts.
labour.evidence_limit: Abstract-level evidence cannot sustain occupational displacement or social-welfare claims.

cases.title: Ile-Ife glass: local primary production within exchange networks
cases.period: Primarily eleventh–fifteenth centuries CE; later Osogbo comparison remains a lead
cases.summary: Chemical groups, crucibles and semi-finished batch support local glassmaking; they do not settle all origins or organisation questions.

stages.invention: Distinct local recipe documented; exact first development and external intellectual contributions unresolved.
stages.feasibility: Finished glass and partially reacted batch demonstrate conversion from raw materials, beyond imported-glass remelting.
stages.deployment: Bead-making debris and specialised crucibles document workshop activity.
stages.diffusion: Related glass at other West African sites supports object exchange; craft migration is not thereby proved.
stages.scaling: Many recovered beads and kilogram-scale batch capacities support substantial activity; no annual output estimate.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Imported glass coexisted in the wider setting; analysed local workshop samples cannot measure city-wide preferences.
stages.displacement/reversal: No demonstrated reason or precise date for cessation; later related production may reflect continuity, movement or redevelopment.

cases.counterevidence: Disturbed excavation deposits and museum provenance limit sequencing; local primary production does not logically prove isolation.

episode.technology_configuration: Ile-Ife high-lime/high-alumina and related glass made and worked in crucibles, principally for beads
episode.task: Primary glass formation, colouring and bead manufacture; uses include adornment but buyer-specific priorities remain unmeasured
episode.population: Excavated Igbo Olokun workshop debris and 52 selected analysed beads; additional museum-store fragments; users at other sites inferred from finds
episode.interval: Primarily eleventh–fifteenth centuries CE; later Osogbo comparison remains a lead
contemporary_alternatives: Imported soda-lime glass objects documented elsewhere at Ile-Ife
Secondary working of imported glass is a technically possible route and historically relevant comparator
Other local bead materials are possible demand substitutes; task-specific comparisons not inspected
episode.adoption_measure: Thousands of finds and batch-capacity estimates establish activity; chemistry of 52 selected beads and regional occurrences identify composition/distribution. No annual output or consumer denominator.
episode.observation_limits: Disturbed deposits, small selected chemical sample and museum provenance constrain chronology. Distribution of objects does not demonstrate transmission of manufacturing skill.

actors.chooser: Glassmakers chose materials/processes; purchaser and political control over production remain unknown.
actors.payer: Unknown; bead quantity and prestige association do not identify workshop finance.
actors.operator_maintainer: Raw-material processors, crucible makers, glassmakers and bead workers inferred from production sequence; whether separate people is unknown.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Fuel collectors, surrounding residents and consumers outside the workshop; their outcomes unmeasured.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Unknown; no workshop contracts, rights or coercive institutions established by the inspected analyses.

labour.tasks: Raw-batch preparation, crucible fabrication, firing, colouring and bead forming; may involve overlapping practitioners.
labour.entry_barriers: Thermal/material knowledge, appropriate ceramics and supplies; apprenticeship or restricted access unknown.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Workshop ownership, political control and distribution of returns unresolved.
labour.transition: Broad workshop period and possible later related sites; no artisan/cohort histories.
labour.distribution: No measured income, gender division, occupational harms or ordinary-consumer access.
labour.evidence_limit: Recovered beads and vessel capacities cannot be converted into employment or productivity per worker.

edges.qualification: Meroe experiments establish process-specific ore sensitivity; does not imply every listed ore is usable.

scope.configuration: Production of new iron by ore reduction in the reported Meroe replica experiments

alternatives: Other suitable iron ores may substitute
Imported metal bypasses the primary-reduction task
edges.necessity_rationale: Within primary ore-reduction production of new iron, removing all iron-bearing feedstock prevents that output. This does not require a specific ore deposit, local ownership, or primary smelting rather than buying metal.
edges.dispute: Oolitic ore was promising; not every ore source or mixture was tested.

edges.qualification: Scoped to reconstructed Meroe forced/mixed-draft operation, not all bloomery designs.

scope.configuration: Meroe replica furnace air delivery, tuyères and coordinated handling

alternatives: Other bellows designs and operating rhythms
edges.dispute: Multiple parameters changed; this hardware arrangement is not uniquely necessary.

edges.qualification: Recipe compatibility and reaction residues; exact quarry and sourcing network remain unresolved.

scope.configuration: Ile-Ife raw-batch reaction with feldspar-rich minerals and a lime-bearing component

alternatives: Exact calcium source could be shell or limestone
edges.dispute: Raw-material family is supported; a uniquely identified quarry/source is not.
